coach_says: Recapturing with the queen walks it into a trap: after Bg5 the queen on f6 is attacked and has nowhere to go. e7 and d8 are on the same diagonal as the bishop, f5 and g6 are covered by Bd3, h6 and f4 by Bg5, and e5 by the d4 pawn, so you lose the queen for a minor piece. gxf6 looks ugly but keeps your material; before recapturing with the queen, check where it goes if it is attacked next move.

Be3 puts your bishop next to the knight on c3, and both stand on squares a black pawn on d4 would hit. Black plays ...d5, your bishop on c4 has to move, then ...d4 forks the knight on c3 and the bishop on e3 and wins a piece. When the opponent has a pawn ready to advance with tempo, don't line up two pieces on the squares it will attack; g4, Ba2 or castling kept everything safe.

a4 lets Black push ...b3, kicking your queen off c2 with tempo and getting a protected passed pawn deep in your camp. Then ...Nb4 comes in, aiming at c2 and d3, where the knight forks your king on e1 and the rook on a1. With your king still in the centre, keep the queen guarding those squares (Qd1) rather than giving Black's pawns a free advance.

You are an exchange down, so your chances are an attack with the queen against Black's king. Qf4 allows ...Qe5, which offers the queen trade and at the same time hits your loose rook on a1 down the long diagonal, so you have to swap queens into a worse endgame. Rc1 first takes the rook off that diagonal and puts it to work against c7, keeping the queens on.
also: keep queens on when behind in material

coach_says: Bxc7 was a free pawn that also hits the rook on d8, winning back the pawn you are down. Ng5 makes no real threat, and it leaves b2 hanging: after ...Bxb2 Rab1 Bc3 the bishop also attacks your rook on e1, a square your knight on e4 used to guard. Before a knight trip, look for loose pawns you can take with tempo, and check what the knight was protecting.

Black's knight on a6 is on its way to c5, where it hits your bishop and eyes e4. Bxa6 bxa6 removes it and leaves Black with doubled, isolated a-pawns and a weak c6, and then c4 opens lines while Black's king is exposed. You are two pawns down, so you need active play; g3 is a slow move that lets ...Nc5 in for free.

With White's pawn on e5, this is a French-type structure where your counterplay comes from hitting d4 with ...c5, or ...dxc4 first to gain time on the bishop. b6 is slow and loosens c6 and the long diagonal to a8; after cxd5 cxd5 the c-file is open and White's queen on c2 stares at your bishop on c8, so tricks like Bg5 appear. Break at the base of the pawn chain before White finishes developing.

The knight on f3 is the piece holding d4. ...g4 kicks it: if it retreats to d2 or e1, ...Qxd4+ wins the pawn with check, so White has to trade with Ne5, the queens come off and you keep a clean extra pawn. Bxc3 instead gives up your bishop for the knight, and bxc3 strengthens d4 and opens the b-file for White. Before trading, look for a move that attacks the defender of a weak pawn.
also: gave up the bishop pair for nothing

coach_says: Castling long puts your king on c1, where the dark squares are weak: you've played b3 and traded your dark-squared bishop, so ...Ba3+ is always there. It also leaves f2 with no defender, and Black's ...e5 hits d4 while opening the c8 bishop onto your queen on g4. Keep the queen active with Qh3 or Qg3 and get the king to the kingside instead.

You are two pawns down in this gambit, so you need to keep the initiative. Ng5 is a lone piece with no real threat; Black just plays ...d6 and castles, and the knight has to go back. e5 instead kicks the knight from f6 with tempo, grabs space and stops Black from freeing himself with ...d5. Use pawn moves that gain time before sending one piece forward on its own.

The h-file is open, Black's rook sits on h8, and the bishop on e6 already aims at h3, the only pawn in front of your king. Qa4 takes your queen to the far side, and ...Bxh3 gxh3 Rxh3+ breaks your king open before you can collect the a5 bishop. Bg4 would have traded off that dangerous bishop; when the opponent has lines toward your king, deal with that before going after material.
Good move: your queen was attacked and Qe2 keeps it safe while still guarding the kingside. Nb5 looked active but lets Black swap queens with ...Rxg4 into a much easier position.
Nxc3 is fine: you grab the pawn and the knight comes back to e4. Developing with ...Bf5 was a touch more natural, but there's nothing to fix here.
Bd3 is a normal developing move, about as good as Be2 or Be3. Just keep an eye on ...e5 and ...Nc5 hitting the bishop later.
Nd5 is reasonable and the position stays balanced. Castling first was slightly simpler, but the difference is small.
e6 is a solid opening choice. It closes in your light-squared bishop a little, which is why some players prefer ...Nf6 or ...Bf5 first, but it's fine.
The position was already lost after the earlier sacrifices; recapturing with the bishop, king or knight are all about the same here.
Rg5 is the best try, hitting the queen and lining up on the g-file. You're worse, but this move is fine.
Rd2+ is fine: the rook gets active on the second rank with check. You stay clearly better.
Bg5 is a good move: it dodges ...Nxf4 and keeps the bishop. Be3 was equally fine.
